attrs.why: New laboratory findings show markedly elevated ACTH, low cortisol, and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, DOC, and androstenedione; expert analysis confirms these support congenital adrenal hyperplasia and the markedly elevated DOC specifically points to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. This strengthens the original virilization, hyperpigmentation, hypertension, and sibling history reasoning, so confidence rises from 0.85 to 0.95.

New laboratory pattern argues against adrenal virilizing tumor: high ACTH with low cortisol is not typical for an autonomous adrenal tumor, and markedly elevated DOC is characteristic of 11β-hydroxylase deficiency CAH rather than a virilizing adrenal tumor. Hyperpigmentation, hypertension, and sibling history also remain atypical, so confidence falls from 0.10 to 0.02.

New laboratory findings show adrenal steroid excess with elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, DOC, and androstenedione plus high ACTH and low cortisol, which is not consistent with central precocious puberty; prepubertal testes, absent pubic hair, hyperpigmentation, and hypertension already refuted this. Confidence falls from 0.05 to 0.01.

attrs.why: The combination of markedly elevated DOC with elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androstenedione, high ACTH, low cortisol, hypertension, hyperpigmentation, virilization, and a sibling with similar symptoms is most consistent with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency CAH; expert analysis notes DOC elevation specifically supports this subtype. Confidence is 0.9 because CYP11B1 sequencing, electrolytes, renin/aldosterone, and adrenal imaging are not yet available.

This corroborates the pre-existing virilization, hyperpigmentation, hypertension, and affected sibling findings. With the affected sibling and characteristic biochemistry also arguing against it, confidence falls from 0.02 to 0.01.

node-17.label: Peripheral precocious puberty due to adrenal androgen excess

attrs.why: The virilization (penile enlargement with facial acne) occurs in a 21-month-old with prepubertal testes and no pubic hair, which indicates androgen exposure not driven by central gonadal activation. Elevated androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone point to an adrenal source of androgens, and the confirmed congenital adrenal hyperplasia supplies that adrenal androgen excess. This distinguishes it from central precocious puberty, whose hypothesis is refuted by the prepubertal testes and the adrenal steroid pattern. Confidence is 0.65 because the classic pubic-hair component is absent and the picture is dominated by the underlying adrenal disorder.
